item.title: qLevelPlace: A Level-Based Placement Framework for RSFQ Circuits
item.description: arXiv:2611.04019v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rapid Single Flux Quantum (RSFQ) logic can operate at ultra-high clock frequencies; however, its physical design is complicated by explicit splitter trees and deep gate-level pipelines in which every logic gate is clocked. To address this challenge, we present qLevelPlace, a level-based placement framework for RSFQ circuits. We separate gate and splitter placement into two stages to better support levelguided gate-to-row assignment and use a timing-aware quadratic cost function to penalize long interconnects. Experiments on the benchmark circuits show that, on average, qLevelPlace achieves a $2.65\times$ higher clock frequency and a 51% reduction in layout area compared with the state-of-the-art RSFQ placer qPlace.
item.dc:creator: Ziyu Liu, Jingkai Hong, Robert S. Aviles, Sasan Razmkhah, Peter A. Beerel, Massoud Pedram

item.title: A signal-processing cascade linking satellite heat exposure, genomic variation, and mortality risk
item.description: arXiv:2611.03667v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Heat-related mortality varies among individuals under similar environmental conditions, yet environmental exposure and genetic susceptibility are typically modelled separately. We propose a signal-processing cascade linking satellite-derived land-surface temperature to sequence-dependent heat-shock response and mortality risk. The framework combines distributed-lag filtering of thermal exposure, nonlinear HSF1 activation, cross-correlation with an HSF1 position-weight-matrix kernel, and Hill-model mapping of sequence-dependent binding changes to regulatory response. Applied to 52 heat-response genes and 157 naturally occurring variants, the framework identifies 21 heat-shock-element arrays across 17 genes. Variants in canonical arrays are significantly enriched for predicted binding disruption ($p=3\times10^{-4}$). Propagating these effects through the cascade yields a peak predicted mortality-risk multiplier of $1.68\times$ at $40$--$42\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The framework demonstrates how environmental and genomic signals can be integrated to model inter-individual variation in heat-related risk.
item.dc:creator: Usman Nazir, Sara Khalid

item.title: Whose startup does the AI back? An algorithm audit of reputation and demographic signals in LLM-assisted crowdfunding
item.description: arXiv:2611.03993v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language model (LLM) assistants increasingly advise backers on which crowdfunding campaigns to support. LLMs have known race and gender problems, and it is unsettled whether they reproduce, erase, or reverse the discrimination documented in entrepreneurial finance. We ask when, and through which decision process, LLM assistants use founders' gender and ethnicity. In a pre-specified choice-based conjoint experiment, seven LLMs chose among five synthetic campaigns with independently randomized quality signals and founder names, under three backer personas and a persona-free control (40,248 responses). By default, founder names barely matter: under budget-conscious and delivery-focused personas, gender and Black-name effects are statistically equivalent to zero. When the backer wants to support underrepresented creators, the models favor Black-signaled (+8.1 percentage points; positive in all seven models) and female-signaled (+5.1) founders. They do so most strongly among near-tied campaigns and for the founder who alone carries the signal, and they almost never name gender or ethnicity in their reasons. The results fit an agency account of algorithmic discrimination: an aligned assistant takes its demographic preferences from its user rather than from its training data.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Journal of Business Venturing Insights 26 (2026) e00682
item.dc:creator: Mirza Samad Ahmed Baig, Syeda Anshrah Gillani

item.title: Edge AI and TinyML for Resource-Constrained Agriculture: Hardware Platforms, Model Optimization, and Deployment Strategies
item.description: arXiv:2603.15085v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Deploying artificial intelligence at the edge is increasingly important for systems that must operate under strict limits on memory, computation, energy, connectivity, and hardware cost. Tiny Machine Learning (TinyML) represents the most resource-constrained regime of this shift, enabling inference on microcontroller-class devices with tightly bounded flash and SRAM budgets. This study examines recent deployment trends in Edge AI and TinyML using precision farming as a representative real-world environment in which sensing nodes, gateways, UAVs, and embedded processors must often operate with intermittent connectivity and limited power. The analysis emphasizes the deployment stack rather than predictive accuracy alone, covering hardware classes, software toolchains, model- and system-level optimization, intelligence placement, and hardware-resource reporting. Across the analyzed studies, microcontroller-class platforms such as ESP32, STM32, and ATmega are prominent endpoint targets, while single-board computers and embedded accelerators support more compute-intensive workloads. Among the studies included in the optimization comparison, almost 50% report quantization, making reduced-precision inference the most frequently identified strategy within this subset. In contrast, structured pruning, hardware-aware neural architecture search, and coordinated cross-layer optimization remain comparatively limited. Resource profiling is also inconsistent as flash, peak RAM, MAC count, latency, and energy per inference are not reported uniformly, limiting reproducibility and comparisons across deployments. A recurring systems-level pattern is an inference-training asymmetry in which inference moves toward local devices while training and model lifecycle management remain predominantly centralized.
item.dc:creator: Riya Samanta, Bidyut Saha, Soumya Kanti Ghosh

item.title: Hardware-Aware Model Inversion in Memristive Spiking Neural Networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.39688v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Hardware-accelerated spiking neural networks (SNNs) implemented on memristive crossbar arrays offer significant gains in energy efficiency, while device variability and analog noise are sometimes assumed to hinder information extraction. However, whether these hardware effects improve, preserve, or degrade privacy after deployment remains largely unexplored. Therefore, we ask whether model-inversion leakage characterized on an SNN remains representative after the same model is mapped to a non-ideal memristive substrate, and how hardware non-idealities and reliability faults affecting synapses, neuron thresholds, and spike processing reshape that leakage. To study this problem, we introduce Spiking Domain Model Inversion (SDMI), an inversion method that combines Expectation over Transformation (EOT) with surrogate gradients to optimize inputs through stochastic analog behavior and non-differentiable spiking dynamics. We use SDMI consistently across the SNN model, its memristive SNN, and the same memristive SNN under additional hardware perturbations. Across four datasets, reconstruction leakage does not vary monotonically with model accuracy or hardware variability. At comparable accuracy levels, neuron-threshold perturbations increase reconstruction fidelity, measured by SSIM, by up to 51.8%, whereas spike-level perturbations primarily degrade utility without consistently improving reconstruction. Weight noise, in contrast, reduces leakage under the same inversion procedure. These results show that hardware variability is not inherently privacy-preserving: model inversion leakage in memristive SNNs depends on the hardware state and cannot be inferred from model accuracy alone.
item.dc:creator: Pablo Sorrentino, Fernando M. Quintana, Erika Covi, Fatih Turkmen
